vulnerabilities.title: NEW TO KEV YESTERDAY WITH A SATURDAY DEADLINE AND A PUBLIC EXPLOIT: Vates Xen Orchestra CVE-2026-133469 Lets an Unauthenticated Attacker Become Administrator by Sending a Login Token Containing an EMPTY JSON OBJECT - CVSS 9.8, Fixed in 6.9.2 and 6.10.1, and Vates Says Any Confirmed Compromise Requires a FULL REINSTALL Because This Is the Management Plane of a Hypervisor Fleet
affected_products: Vates Xen Orchestra before 6.9.2 (stable branch)
Vates Xen Orchestra before 6.10.1 (latest branch)
Xen Orchestra Appliance (XOA)
XCP-ng and XenServer estates managed through an affected Xen Orchestra instance
vulnerabilities.summary:
This is the most trivially exploitable vulnerability in today's report and it sits on the management plane of virtualisation estates that UK organisations have been migrating to since Broadcom repriced VMware.

WHAT IT IS, AND IT IS AS SIMPLE AS IT SOUNDS. CVE-2026-133469 is an improper authentication flaw (CWE-287) in Xen Orchestra's REST API handling of the login cookie. An unauthenticated attacker authenticates as an administrator by presenting a login token that contains nothing at all - an empty JSON object. There is no credential to guess, no race to win, no memory corruption to tune, and no payload to deliver. It is a single crafted cookie. CVSS 9.8. One tracker states the flaw enables authentication and multi-factor authentication bypass leading to administrative takeover of Xen Orchestra and root remote code execution on the managed XCP-ng or XenServer hypervisors; the MFA bypass follows logically from an authentication check that is never reached, but the root RCE claim is single-sourced and is not carried here as established. It does not need to be. Administrative control of Xen Orchestra is already sufficient to create, clone, snapshot, export or destroy every virtual machine in the estate, and to read the backup repositories.

WHY UK ORGANISATIONS ARE DISPROPORTIONATELY IN SCOPE RIGHT NOW. Xen Orchestra is the management plane for XCP-ng, and XCP-ng has been the principal open-source destination for organisations leaving VMware since Broadcom's licensing changes. UK local government, universities, NHS trusts and mid-market corporates have been running exactly that migration through 2025 and 2026, under cost pressure, frequently with the new platform stood up by a small team alongside the old one. Migration-era infrastructure has a predictable security profile: it is newer than the documentation, outside the established patch cadence, often not yet covered by the monitoring that watches the VMware estate it is replacing, and reachable from more places than it should be because engineers needed access while they built it. That is the population this CVE will find. Note also that rank 1 of this report concerns Drupal sites in 'unusual or incomplete installation states' - the same migration-shaped exposure, in a different layer of the same estates.

THE EXPLOIT AND THE DEADLINE. CISA added CVE-2026-133469 to KEV on 25 November 2026 with a reported federal remediation due date of 28 November 2026. A public proof-of-concept is indexed on exploit aggregators. The fixes are Xen Orchestra 6.9.2 on the stable branch and 6.10.1 on the latest branch. Vates's own guidance goes further than patching and should be read carefully: administrators are advised not to expose Xen Orchestra to the internet at all, and to FULLY REINSTALL any deployment where compromise is confirmed. That second instruction is the vendor stating that it does not consider post-compromise cleanup of this component reliable - which is the correct position for a management plane that holds credentials to every hypervisor it administers, and which means the decision you are making this week is not 'patch or not' but 'patch, or rebuild'.

WHAT AN ATTACKER DOES WITH IT. Administrative access to Xen Orchestra gives snapshot and export of any virtual machine, which is whole-system data theft that never touches a guest operating system and therefore never meets an endpoint agent. It gives access to backup jobs and repositories, which is the standard pre-ransomware step. It gives the ability to create new virtual machines inside a trusted network segment. And because Xen Orchestra stores the credentials it uses to administer its hosts, it gives a credible path onward to the hypervisors themselves regardless of whether the single-sourced root RCE claim is accurate. Virtualisation management compromise is the preferred modern ransomware path precisely because encrypting at the hypervisor layer defeats in-guest protection entirely.

EVIDENCE QUALITY. The vulnerability, the affected ranges and the fixed versions are consistent across many sources, so those are high confidence. The exploitation claim rests on the KEV listing, reported here via aggregators rather than read from CISA's own catalogue - direct retrieval failed in this run, as it has every day this week. No attacker infrastructure, indicator of compromise, hash or attribution has been published. Two cautions for anyone recording this: the CVE identifier's numbering has been flagged as unusual by one tracker, and the Vates advisory references reported in the sources (VSA-2026-062 and GHSA-2r3w-c2vx-fv5g) should be confirmed at source before being used as audit evidence.
recommended_actions: Upgrade to Xen Orchestra 6.9.2 (stable) or 6.10.1 (latest) now. There is no credential requirement, no exploitation complexity and a public proof-of-concept, which puts this in the small category of flaws that opportunistic scanning will convert to compromise within days rather than weeks.

Take Xen Orchestra off the internet, permanently. Vates's own advice is not to expose it at all. A virtualisation management plane has no business being internet-reachable; if remote administration is needed, put it behind a VPN or a privileged access gateway.

Decide now what you will do if you find evidence of compromise, because Vates's answer is a FULL REINSTALL of the deployment. Post-compromise cleanup of a component that holds credentials to every hypervisor it manages is not reliable. Budget and plan for rebuild as the realistic outcome, not patching.

Review Xen Orchestra authentication and REST API logs for successful administrative sessions with no preceding credential validation, and for sessions whose token or cookie was empty or malformed. That is the exact observable shape of this flaw and it is the only high-confidence detection available.

Audit virtual machine snapshot, clone and export activity across the whole estate for the last 60 days. Exporting a VM is complete data theft that never touches the guest operating system and therefore never meets an endpoint agent. If you only review in-guest telemetry you will find nothing and conclude wrongly.

Check backup jobs, backup repositories and their credentials. Access to the backup plane is the standard pre-ransomware step, and Xen Orchestra is the backup orchestrator as well as the management console in most XCP-ng deployments.

Rotate every credential Xen Orchestra holds if there is any doubt: hypervisor administrative accounts, backup repository credentials, storage and SMTP credentials, API tokens and any directory integration. Patching the console and leaving the stored credentials in place closes the door and leaves the keys in it.

Enumerate your post-VMware migration estate specifically, and treat it as a distinct risk population. XCP-ng and Xen Orchestra instances stood up during a VMware exit are typically outside the patch cadence, outside the monitoring scope and more widely reachable than intended. Rank 1 of this report describes the same migration-shaped exposure in the web layer.

Do not downgrade this because the single-sourced hypervisor root RCE claim is unconfirmed. Administrative control of Xen Orchestra alone permits snapshot, export, clone and destruction of every virtual machine in the estate. The impact does not depend on the disputed claim.

Confirm the advisory references before recording remediation. The sources cite VSA-2026-062 and GHSA-2r3w-c2vx-fv5g, and one tracker has flagged the CVE identifier's numbering as unusual. Verify against Vates directly if this is going into an audit file.

kql.query:

| where TimeGenerated > ago(45d)
| where DestinationHostName has_any ("xo", "xoa", "orchestra", "xcp", "xen") or DestinationPort in (443, 80, 3000)
| extend IsExternalSource = not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP))

vulnerabilities.summary:
Three London-listed UK high street names appeared on one extortion leak site inside six days, and the newest two were posted in this reporting window. This entry is about the pattern and the deadline, not about any one retailer.

WHAT HAPPENED IN THIS WINDOW. Ransomware and extortion trackers logged N0n listings for hmv and Next plc on 25 November 2026. Halfords Group plc - the London Stock Exchange-listed automotive and cycling retailer and services business - was listed days earlier, with trackers giving 20 November and 23 November and therefore in conflict; the Halfords listing described the victim only generically as 'automotive and cycling' rather than naming it in the post body. One tracker reports a claimed data volume of 233 GB for Next. The hmv listing describes the claimed data as shopper search sessions with typed queries and related storefront analytics. BreachNews reports the leak site's publication deadline for the new retail entries as around 2 December 2026, which makes next Tuesday the operative date for anyone tracking this.

THE NEXT PLC CASE IS THE ONE TO WATCH, AND HERE IS WHY. On 23 November 2026, through a Regulatory News Service notice, Next plc disclosed that one of its third-party online suppliers had suffered a cyber incident resulting in unauthorised access to certain data relating to the retailer. Next's characterisation was explicit and unusually confident: the information is 'benign', it cannot be used to facilitate fraud against customers or the business, and no customer personal data has been compromised. The supplier was not named. Next said it is working with the supplier, law enforcement and regulatory authorities. Two days later an extortion group listed the company and a tracker reported a claimed 233 GB. Those two positions are not automatically contradictory - 233 GB of low-sensitivity operational data is entirely possible, and extortion groups systematically overstate both volume and sensitivity because their leverage depends on it. But the sequence is the thing to learn from rather than adjudicate: a company made a definitive public assessment of data sensitivity within hours of a supplier incident, and an adversary with a commercial interest in contradicting it published two days later. A UK listed company making a 'benign' determination in an RNS notice before the extortion stage has begun is taking a market-disclosure risk that most of its peers avoid, and the resolution of this one will be visible on 2 December.

CLAIMS ARE NOT CONFIRMATIONS, AND THIS ENTRY IS EXPLICIT ABOUT THAT. None of the three companies has confirmed a breach of its own systems. Halfords has not publicly confirmed an incident and its recent stock exchange announcements do not mention one. hmv has made no statement found in this run. Next has confirmed a SUPPLIER incident, which is not the same as confirming the leak site's claim about what was taken. Everything in this entry that originates from N0n is attacker self-reporting on an extortion platform whose business model rewards exaggeration, which is why the entry carries exploitation status 'exploitation attempts reported unconfirmed' and medium confidence rather than high.

A group posting at that rate across that many countries is not running targeted intrusions against individually selected UK retailers. It is monetising access acquired at scale - most plausibly through shared suppliers, stolen credentials and commodity initial access - which is precisely consistent with rank 4 of this report and with the five-for-five third-party pattern across every confirmed UK consumer disclosure this month. N0n has also named Mattel, Gannett and around twenty other companies in the same period, so UK retail is a slice of indiscriminate volume rather than a campaign.

The useful action is to assume the shared supplier base is the vector - because that is what the November evidence says - and to establish, before a listing appears, what each e-commerce, analytics, communications and fulfilment supplier holds, and who is named as owning that relationship. The second useful action is to pre-agree the disclosure posture. Next's experience shows the cost of a confident early assessment; the opposite error, saying nothing for three weeks, has its own regulatory and reputational price. Deciding which risk you prefer while nothing is happening is considerably cheaper than deciding it at 22:00 on the day a leak site posts your name.

Five consecutive confirmed UK consumer disclosures this month originated at a third party. A group posting at N0n's rate across 48 countries is monetising access acquired at scale, which in practice means suppliers, stolen credentials and commodity initial access - not bespoke intrusions against you.

Watch 2 December 2026. BreachNews reports that as the leak site's publication deadline for the new UK retail entries. If you have any reason to think you are in scope, your communications, legal and regulatory notification decisions need to be made before then, not in response to publication.

Do not make a public sensitivity determination before you can defend it. Next plc stated within hours that supplier-held data was 'benign' and could not facilitate fraud, and was listed by an extortion group two days later with a claimed 233 GB. Both positions may be true, but the sequence shows the risk of a definitive early RNS characterisation. Pre-agree your disclosure posture now, while nothing is happening.

Treat leak-site listings as intelligence, not fact, in your own reporting. None of the three retailers has confirmed a breach of its own systems. Halfords has not publicly confirmed an incident. Attacker self-reporting on an extortion platform is the lowest evidential tier available and it is systematically inflated because leverage depends on it.

Hunt your own environment for the access routes this pattern uses rather than for N0n indicators, because no malware sample, infrastructure or TTP detail has been published for this group. That means credential-based access: impossible-travel and new-country sign-ins on supplier and service accounts, OAuth consent grants to unfamiliar applications, and new credentials added to existing service principals.

Review and constrain what your e-commerce, analytics and storefront suppliers can read. The hmv listing claims shopper search sessions and typed queries - that is storefront analytics data, which sits with a third-party tag or platform, is rarely classified as personal data internally, and is almost never covered by a data retention policy. Typed search queries can be considerably more revealing than the field list suggests.

Ask whether you would even know. In at least two of the five UK November incidents the supplier was not named publicly, and in the Next case the retailer learned of exposure through the supplier. Review contractual notification windows with every supplier holding customer or operational data and push them to hours rather than days. This is a procurement action.

Give your fraud and contact-centre teams advance notice. Whether or not data is ever published, an extortion listing naming a UK high street brand generates immediate secondary activity: phishing referencing the 'breach', fake compensation and refund offers, and credential stuffing against the brand's own accounts on the assumption that something leaked.

For boards: the question to ask management this week is not 'are we on the list'. It is 'name every third party that holds our customer or transaction data, say what fields each holds, and say who owns that relationship'. The November evidence is that the organisations unable to answer that question quickly are the ones that spend three weeks publicly unsure what was taken.

vulnerabilities.title: DISCLOSED IN THIS WINDOW AND IT STARTED WITH ONE HIJACKED EMPLOYEE GITHUB ACCOUNT: 1Password Confirmed on 25 November That an Attacker Pushed Malicious Code Into Its BACKEND SYSTEMS on 19 November and Copied Customer Names, Emails, Account and User IDs - Plus Tokens From INVITATION, PROVISIONING and ACCOUNT RECOVERY Emails - While Vaults Stayed Intact, and the Company Has Now Lengthened Recovery Codes From Six Digits to Ten Alphanumeric Characters
affected_products: 1Password backend systems - account metadata for a subset of customers
Tokens embedded in 1Password invitation, provisioning and account recovery emails
1Password Business and Enterprise tenants using SCIM provisioning or SSO
NOT affected: customer vault contents, which 1Password states remain secure
vulnerabilities.summary:
A password manager used across UK corporate and public sector estates disclosed in this window that an attacker reached its backend through a hijacked employee GitHub account. The vaults held. Almost everything around the vaults did not.

WHAT 1PASSWORD HAS CONFIRMED. On 25 November 2026 the company published an update stating that an attacker hijacked an employee's GitHub account on 19 November 2026 and used it to push malicious code into its backend systems, then copied account data for a subset of customers. The copied data comprises names, email addresses, account IDs, user IDs, account creation dates and last sign-in times. Critically, it also includes TOKENS FROM INVITATION, PROVISIONING AND ACCOUNT RECOVERY EMAILS. 1Password's position on those tokens is that a token only works when combined with an SSO sign-in or a six digit code. The company states that customer vaults were not affected and all vault contents remain secure, and that customers do not need to change anything in their 1Password account. It warns of phishing, specifically unexpected invitation or recovery emails. And it has increased the length of codes used in invitation and account recovery emails from six digits to TEN ALPHANUMERIC CHARACTERS.

READ THAT LAST CHANGE AS THE REAL RISK ASSESSMENT. A company that genuinely believed the stolen tokens were inert would not re-engineer the codes those tokens pair with, in an emergency, days after the incident. Lengthening a six-digit numeric code to ten alphanumeric characters takes the brute-force space from one million to roughly 3.7 x 10^15 - a change of about nine orders of magnitude. That is the action of an organisation that has concluded the surviving control was a six-digit code and that a six-digit code is not enough when the attacker already holds the matching token, the account ID, the user ID and the email address. The honest reading of this incident is therefore: the vault encryption architecture did its job exactly as designed, and the account lifecycle around it - invitations, provisioning, recovery - is where the residual risk sits. For a UK business or public body, the practical exposure is account takeover through a forged or replayed invitation or recovery flow, not decryption of anybody's vault.

THE INITIAL ACCESS ROUTE IS THE PART EVERY UK ORGANISATION SHOULD ACT ON. One employee's GitHub account was hijacked and that was sufficient to push code into production backend systems. That is the same category of failure as rank 4 and rank 7 of this report, moved one layer down the stack: the compromise did not arrive through the product, it arrived through the development and deployment pipeline. Whatever controls stood between a developer's personal source-control credential and running backend code were insufficient - and that question is answerable in your own organisation this afternoon. Can a single compromised developer identity get code into production? Are branch protection, mandatory review, signed commits, and phishing-resistant MFA enforced on every account with write access to anything that deploys? For most UK organisations the answer is less comfortable than they expect, and this incident is the cheapest possible prompt to find out.

THE DISCLOSURE TIMING IS A LEGITIMATE CRITICISM. The account was hijacked on 19 November; the disclosure came on 25 November. MacRumors noted that the breach was not disclosed when 1Password first learned of it and that it is unclear whether 1Password has notified all affected users. Six days of silence on stolen account-recovery tokens is six days in which customers could not watch for the exact phishing the company is now warning them about. UK organisations should factor that into their own supplier assessment of 1Password, and should also note it as a precedent for their own disclosure decisions - the same tension that rank 7 shows from the opposite direction, where Next plc disclosed within hours and made a confident assessment it may yet have to revisit.

EVIDENCE QUALITY. This is one of the better-evidenced entries in today's report: the primary source is the vendor's own published incident update, corroborated by consistent reporting across multiple outlets. What is NOT established: the number or identity of affected customers ('a subset' is the company's own wording), whether any stolen token has actually been used, how the employee's GitHub account was hijacked in the first place, what the pushed malicious code did beyond enabling data copying, whether the attacker had access between 19 and 25 November, and whether notification has reached all affected users. No attacker attribution, infrastructure or indicator of compromise has been published, so defensive action is preventative rather than detective.
recommended_actions: Answer this question in your own organisation today: can a single compromised developer identity get code into production? One hijacked employee GitHub account was enough here. Verify that branch protection, mandatory independent review, signed commits and phishing-resistant MFA are enforced on every account with write access to anything that deploys - not just on the main branch of your flagship repository.

Treat ALL unexpected 1Password invitation, provisioning and account recovery emails as hostile until verified out of band. The attacker holds tokens from exactly those email types alongside the matching account IDs, user IDs, names and email addresses. This is the one concrete, immediate action for every 1Password customer.

Audit your 1Password tenant's membership and provisioning changes since 19 November 2026: new members added, recovery initiated, SCIM provisioning changes, group membership changes, and any administrative role grant. The stolen token types map directly onto those operations.

Review your SSO configuration and conditional access for the 1Password application specifically. The company states a stolen token only works when combined with an SSO sign-in or a six digit code, which makes the SSO path one of the two remaining controls. Enforce device compliance and phishing-resistant authentication on that application if you have not.

Read the code-length change as the vendor's own risk assessment and act accordingly. Increasing invitation and recovery codes from six digits to ten alphanumeric characters is roughly a nine-order-of-magnitude change in brute-force space, executed in an emergency. It indicates the vendor concluded a six-digit code was the surviving control and was not sufficient against an attacker holding the matching token.

Do NOT mass-rotate every credential in your vaults. 1Password states vault contents were not affected and that customers need not change anything in their account. A panic rotation of thousands of secrets creates outages, lockouts and shadow copies in spreadsheets, which is a larger real risk than the one being mitigated. Rotate on evidence, not on anxiety.

Brief your staff before the phishing arrives, with specific wording. The credible lure is an email that correctly uses the recipient's name and email address and references their real 1Password account, asking them to accept an invitation or complete a recovery. Tell people the exact shape of the message, not a generic 'beware of phishing' note.

Add the disclosure timing to your supplier assessment record: hijack on 19 November, disclosure on 25 November, and public uncertainty over whether all affected users have been notified. Six days of silence on stolen account-recovery tokens is six days customers could not watch for the phishing they are now being warned about.

For UK organisations that use a password manager as the control compensating for weak credential hygiene elsewhere: note what actually protected customers here. It was the encryption architecture - vaults encrypted with keys the vendor never holds - not the vendor's perimeter. Architectural controls survived a backend compromise. Operational ones did not.

Extend the lesson to every SaaS vendor whose source control you depend on. The question is not whether you trust 1Password. It is which of your suppliers could have production code altered by one compromised developer account, and whether you have ever asked any of them.

vulnerabilities.summary:
This entry exists because the calendar has become the risk. Three separate CISA KEV remediation deadlines now fall inside 72 hours, covering between thirteen and fifteen actively exploited vulnerabilities depending on how the contested 25 November batch is counted. Two expire TODAY. For a UK organisation none of these dates is legally binding - the Binding Operational Directive applies to US federal civilian agencies - but they are the clearest external signal available of how urgently a national authority assesses each flaw, and a UK security function that cannot say which of these thirteen-plus flaws it is exposed to by Saturday does not have a vulnerability management function, it has a scanner.

EXPIRING TODAY, 26 NOVEMBER. Both were added on 23 November. CVE-2026-133968 in Project MONAI Label 0.8.5 and earlier is a path traversal flaw at CVSS 9.8 allowing an unauthenticated remote attacker to write files outside the intended datastore directory, which can lead to remote code execution; the fix is 0.8.6, and reported exploitation PREDATES the 20 November disclosure. This one matters specifically to UK NHS trusts and university medical imaging research groups, because MONAI is the dominant open-source medical imaging AI framework and MONAI Label is its annotation server - typically stood up by a research team on departmental infrastructure, outside the trust's managed estate, holding imaging data. Note the scoping precision: the advisory does not establish that the core MONAI framework is affected, only MONAI Label. CVE-2026-134624 in N-able MailAssure, formerly SpamExperts, is a server-side request forgery allowing an authenticated, highly privileged API user to make the server connect to arbitrary internal hosts and ports; fixed in build 20261121.1943. MailAssure is a mail filtering platform sold heavily through the managed service provider channel, which is the same downstream-visibility problem as rank 3 - UK organisations consuming it as part of a managed mail service cannot patch it and may not know they use it.

EXPIRING TOMORROW, 27 NOVEMBER. Three, all added on 24 November. CVE-2026-132165, the Drupal core installer RCE - and this is where today's report requires you to look at rank 1, because the remediation for this deadline was SUPERSEDED on 25 November by SA-CORE-2026-019. Patching to 10.6.22, 11.3.22 or 11.4.13 satisfies the letter of this deadline and leaves you exposed to a second exploited flaw in the same file. Do not close this deadline on the superseded build. CVE-2026-132224, the Optimizely Web Experimentation signup-flow abuse that let an attacker write Project JavaScript served from Optimizely's own CDN to at least 178 organisations including the BBC, HSBC, TalkTalk, Zoom, IKEA, Salesforce and CNN during a window on 16 November beginning around 04:21 UTC; remediation is vendor-side and Optimizely says the flaw is fixed, but the company has not said how many projects were altered or whether the intruder retains access. A caution on this one: searches in this run did not re-confirm the CVE identifier CVE-2026-132224 against a primary source, so that identifier is carried forward from this feed's 25 November entry and should be verified before it goes into an audit record. And CVE-2026-131914 in Idunno.AntiCsrf, which is the one to put in front of a governance board: it is actively exploited, it is on KEV with a deadline tomorrow, AND NO PATCH EXISTS OR WILL EVER BE ISSUED. The only compliant remediation is removing the component. A mandated deadline against an unpatchable abandoned library is the purest available illustration of the real problem - the dependency nobody owns.

EXPIRING SATURDAY, 28 NOVEMBER. The contested batch of 25 November, covering Mitel MiCollab (five CVEs), HPE Juniper Session Smart (CVE-2026-103406), Danfoss AK-SM 800A (three CVEs) and Vates Xen Orchestra (CVE-2026-133469) - ranks 2, 3, 5 and 6 of this report. The split is genuinely contested: most sources say eight of ten are due 28 November with two due 9 December; one says the five Mitel entries are all due 9 December; another describes the batch as nine entries with seven due 28 November. Plan to the earliest date in your own estate and stop trying to reconcile the sources.

ALREADY OVERDUE AND NOT PUBLICLY RESOLVED. Four earlier deadlines have passed with no published follow-up in any source reviewed: 23 November (CVE-2026-123890, the VMware vCenter authentication bypass at CVSS 9.8 linked to a China-nexus intrusion set, where vCenter 7.0 is reported to have no public fix), 24 November (CVE-2026-20320 and CVE-2026-76466, the Cisco BroadWorks and Expressway flaws), and CVE-2026-124194, the Outlook zero-day used to steal NTLM hashes from the November Patch Tuesday. Overdue items receive no further publicity, which means they drop out of threat intelligence feeds while remaining exactly as exploited as they were on the day of listing. If your organisation's KEV tracking is driven by news coverage rather than by the catalogue, these four are already invisible to you.

WHAT TO DO WITH THIS ENTRY. Not read it. Use it as a checklist, today, and answer one question per line: are we exposed, yes or no. Thirteen to fifteen actively exploited flaws across a CMS, a medical imaging annotation server, a mail filtering platform, an experimentation CDN, an abandoned anti-CSRF library, a unified communications suite, an SD-WAN orchestration plane, supermarket refrigeration controllers and a hypervisor management console. There is no common technology and no common vendor. The only thing that gets an organisation through a week like this is an accurate inventory, which is also the second of the two control gaps the NCSC named on 24 November.
recommended_actions: Work the board as a checklist today and record a yes or no for each: MONAI Label 0.8.5 or earlier, N-able MailAssure below build 20261121.1943, Drupal core, Optimizely Web Experimentation, Idunno.AntiCsrf, Mitel MiCollab, Juniper Session Smart, Danfoss AK-SM 800A, Vates Xen Orchestra. Nine questions. A security function that cannot answer them by Saturday has a scanner, not a vulnerability management capability.

DO NOT close the 27 November Drupal deadline on the superseded build. CVE-2026-132165's remediation was superseded on 25 November by SA-CORE-2026-019 and CVE-2026-136716. Patching to 10.6.22 / 11.3.22 / 11.4.13 meets the letter of this deadline and leaves a second exploited flaw open in the same file. Go to 10.6.23 / 11.3.23 / 11.4.14 - see rank 1.

Ask your NHS trust or university research computing team today whether MONAI Label is running anywhere, and on what version. The deadline is TODAY, the flaw is unauthenticated path traversal to remote code execution at CVSS 9.8, exploitation predates disclosure, and the typical deployment is a research team's annotation server on departmental infrastructure outside the managed estate, holding imaging data. The fix is 0.8.6.

Scope MONAI correctly. The advisory does not establish that the core MONAI framework is affected - MONAI Label is a separate application in the wider ecosystem. Do not raise a change against every MONAI dependency in the estate, and do not let that scoping nuance delay patching the Label servers.

Ask your managed service provider about N-able MailAssure today, in writing. The deadline is TODAY and MailAssure sells heavily through the MSP channel, which means many UK organisations consume it inside a managed mail service, cannot patch it, and may not know they use it. The fix is build 20261121.1943. Same written-question approach as rank 3.

Put CVE-2026-131914 in front of a governance board, not an engineering team. Idunno.AntiCsrf is actively exploited, carries a KEV deadline tomorrow, and HAS NO PATCH AND NEVER WILL. The only compliant remediation is deleting the component. This is the unowned-dependency problem in its purest form and it is a governance decision about accepted risk, not a patching task.

Verify the Optimizely CVE identifier before using it as audit evidence. Searches in this run did not re-confirm CVE-2026-132224 against a primary source; it is carried forward from this feed's 25 November entry. Remediation is vendor-side in any case - the customer-side action is reviewing what your Project JavaScript served on 16 November and whether your Content Security Policy would have helped (it would not have, because the code came from an allowlisted domain).

Plan the Saturday batch to the EARLIEST reported date and stop reconciling the sources. Most accounts say eight of ten due 28 November with two due 9 December; one says all five Mitel entries are due 9 December; another counts nine entries with seven due 28 November. The conflict is unresolvable from available sources and is irrelevant to a UK organisation, which is bound by none of the dates.

Re-open the four OVERDUE items, because nobody else will: CVE-2026-123890 (VMware vCenter authentication bypass, CVSS 9.8, China-nexus exploitation, vCenter 7.0 reported to have no public fix), CVE-2026-20320 and CVE-2026-76466 (Cisco BroadWorks and Expressway), and CVE-2026-124194 (Outlook zero-day, NTLM hash theft). Overdue items lose news coverage while remaining exactly as exploited. If your KEV tracking follows headlines rather than the catalogue, these are already invisible to you.

Fix the structural problem this entry describes, not just the thirteen flaws. Nine product families, no common vendor, no common technology, three deadlines in 72 hours. The only thing that gets an organisation through this is an accurate inventory of public-facing and internet-adjacent systems - which is exactly the second control gap the NCSC named on 24 November, alongside throttled sign-ups.

kql.name: Estate sweep for every product family on the deadline board
kql.description: One query to answer the nine-question checklist against observed network traffic rather than against a CMDB that will be wrong.
kql.query:
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| extend Family = case(
    DestinationHostName has_any ("monai", "monailabel", "annotat", "imaging", "radiol", "pacs"), "MONAI Label (DUE TODAY)",
    DestinationHostName has_any ("mailassure", "spamexperts", "antispam", "mailfilter", "mx"), "N-able MailAssure (DUE TODAY)",
    RequestURL has_any ("install.php", "/core/", "/sites/default"), "Drupal (DUE TOMORROW)",
    DestinationHostName has_any ("optimizely", "cdn.optimizely"), "Optimizely (DUE TOMORROW)",
    DestinationHostName has_any ("micollab", "awv", "mitel"), "Mitel MiCollab (SATURDAY)",
    DestinationHostName has_any ("conductor", "session-smart", "ssr"), "Juniper Session Smart (SATURDAY)",
    DestinationHostName has_any ("ak-sm", "danfoss", "refrig", "chiller"), "Danfoss AK-SM (SATURDAY)",
    DestinationHostName has_any ("xoa", "orchestra", "xcp"), "Xen Orchestra (SATURDAY)",
    "other")
| where Family != "other"
| summarize Sessions = count(), Hosts = make_set(DestinationHostName, 20), ExternalSources = dcountif(SourceIP, not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP))) by Family
| order by ExternalSources desc

kql.name: MONAI Label datastore path traversal attempts - deadline is TODAY
kql.description: CVE-2026-133968 writes files outside the intended datastore directory. Traversal sequences against datastore and upload endpoints are the signature, and exploitation predates the 20 November disclosure so hunt back further.
kql.query:
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where csUriStem has_any ("/datastore", "/upload", "/annotation", "/label", "/infer", "/session")
| where csUriStem has_any ("..", "%2e%2e", "%252e", "..%2f", "..\\") or csUriQuery has_any ("..", "%2e%2e", "%252e")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, cUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

kql.name: Files written outside the MONAI datastore directory
kql.description: The post-exploitation artefact for the path traversal. A file written by the MONAI process outside its datastore tree is the finding, and a script or executable extension makes it a code execution finding.
kql.query:
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python", "python3", "uvicorn", "gunicorn", "monailabel")
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified")
| where not(FolderPath has_any ("datastore", "/tmp", "site-packages", "__pycache__", "/proc", "/var/log"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

kql.name: MailAssure SSRF - outbound connections from the mail filter to internal hosts
kql.description: CVE-2026-134624 makes the server connect to arbitrary internal hosts and ports. A mail filtering platform reaching into the internal estate on non-mail ports is the detection.
kql.query:
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
| where SourceHostName has_any ("mailassure", "spamexperts", "mailfilter", "antispam") or SourceIP in (dynamic([]))
| where ipv4_is_private(DestinationIP)
| where DestinationPort !in (25, 465, 587, 993, 995, 143, 110, 53)
| summarize Attempts = count(), Ports = make_set(DestinationPort, 25), Targets = dcount(DestinationIP), TargetSample = make_set(DestinationIP, 25) by SourceHostName, SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 1d)
| order by Targets desc

kql.name: Find the Idunno.AntiCsrf dependency you cannot patch
kql.description: CVE-2026-131914 has no patch and the only remediation is removal. Locating the component is therefore the entire task, and it is a .NET library that will not appear in any product inventory.
kql.query:
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where csUriStem endswith ".aspx" or csUriStem has_any ("/api/", "antiforgery", "csrf", "__RequestVerificationToken")
| summarize Requests = count(), Paths = make_set(csUriStem, 20), ExternalClients = dcountif(cIP, not(ipv4_is_private(cIP))) by Computer, sSiteName
| where ExternalClients > 0
| order by ExternalClients desc

kql.name: Locate Idunno.AntiCsrf assemblies on disk for deletion
kql.description: The only compliant remediation is deleting the DLL. This finds it across the estate so the governance decision has an inventory behind it.
kql.query:
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(180d)
| where FileName has_any ("Idunno.AntiCsrf", "AntiCsrf", "Idunno")
| summarize Events = count(), Paths = make_set(FolderPath, 30), Actions = make_set(ActionType, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, FileName
| order by LastSeen desc

kql.name: Correlate existing alerts against the whole deadline board

vulnerabilities.vendor: UK Parliament / Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
affected_products: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill - Bill 4035
Lords Amendment 107 - a yearly review of the NIS regime
Lords Amendment 108 - a register of foreign powers
UK operators of essential services and relevant digital service providers under the NIS Regulations
Managed service providers and designated critical suppliers who would be brought into scope
vulnerabilities.summary:
Every other entry in today's report is an operational problem. This one is the governance context they all sit inside, and the timing is unusually pointed: in the same week that a Gatwick payments supplier, an unnamed Next plc online supplier and a supermarket refrigeration estate all produced UK cyber incidents, Parliament was arguing about how widely to draw the regime that would cover them.

WHAT HAPPENED. Official Parliament pages list consideration of Lords amendments to the Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill for 24 November 2026 - not 25 November, and this feed's 25 November entry framed the outcome as reported rather than confirmed, which remains the correct framing. The two amendments at issue are Lords Amendment 107, a yearly review of the NIS regime, and Lords Amendment 108, a register of foreign powers. The Government tabled motions asking MPs to disagree with both. Unofficial trackers report that on 24 November the Commons rejected both Lords defeats, voting 260 to 98 against the register of foreign powers, and that the Bill therefore returns to the Lords. That outcome could NOT be confirmed against an official source in this run - Hansard and the Parliament Bills pages were not retrievable, as no page fetch succeeded in this run at all - so it is carried at medium confidence. The Lords had previously voted 202 to 155 for a review of the whole NIS regime. Separately, the Bill's carry-over has been extended and it now lapses if not passed by the end of 29 April 2027.

WHY A SECURITY TEAM SHOULD CARE RATHER THAN SKIP THIS. Two reasons, and the first is immediate. The Bill's central purpose is to extend the NIS regulatory perimeter beyond directly designated operators to managed service providers and designated critical suppliers. Look at what this report contains. Rank 4: a designated CNI airport, breached through Times24 UK Limited, its drop-off charge processor. Rank 7: Next plc, breached through an unnamed online supplier. Rank 3: UK organisations consuming Juniper SD-WAN through managed service providers who cannot patch it themselves. Rank 9: N-able MailAssure consumed through the MSP channel. Rank 5: refrigeration controllers owned by facilities contractors and sitting in no IT register. Five of today's ten entries turn on an organisation being compromised, or being unable to act, because the relevant technology or data sat with a third party. That is precisely the gap the Bill addresses, and it remains open.

The second reason is the clock. The carry-over extension to 29 April 2027 is the operationally significant detail, and it cuts in a specific direction. It means there is no near-term regulatory deadline forcing UK boards to act - the Bill may receive Royal Assent in weeks or may consume another five months of parliamentary time - while the underlying risk is accumulating at the rate the rest of this report documents. Organisations waiting for the statutory duty before investing in supply chain assurance will be waiting, on this timetable, through at least one more winter of exactly these incidents. The practical instruction is to build third-party assurance now against the regime's known direction of travel rather than against its final text, because every substantive version of this Bill has pointed the same way: wider scope, supplier accountability, faster incident reporting.

AND THE TWO REJECTED AMENDMENTS ARE WORTH UNDERSTANDING ON THEIR MERITS. Amendment 107, a yearly review of the NIS regime, addresses the problem that produced the Bill in the first place - the regime it amends dates from 2018 and had no mechanism to keep pace with a threat picture that the NCSC itself described on 3 November as one in which UK cyber resilience is falling behind, with 80 nationally significant incidents recorded. A statutory annual review is a slow instrument, but the alternative evidenced by the last eight years is no instrument. Amendment 108, a register of foreign powers, speaks directly to a UK posture that was publicly stated in this same month: on 20 November the head of the Cyber and Specialist Operations Command confirmed offensive cyber operations, and the UK confirmed around 23 November that these were directed against Russia, China, Iran and North Korea. A Government that names four hostile states in public while declining a statutory register of foreign powers is making a deliberate choice about flexibility versus transparency; whether that is the right choice is a political question, but security teams should understand that it is the choice being made.

EVIDENCE QUALITY, STATED PLAINLY. Medium confidence throughout, and the reason is methodological rather than substantive. The scheduling of consideration of Lords amendments for 24 November 2026, the identity of Amendments 107 and 108, the Government's motions to disagree, the prior Lords vote of 202 to 155 and the 29 April 2027 carry-over date all come from official Parliament pages as surfaced through search. The outcome - both amendments rejected, the 260 to 98 division, the return to the Lords - comes from unofficial tracking sites only. Hansard should be checked directly before any of the division figures are quoted in a board paper or compliance document.
recommended_actions: Check Hansard for 24 November 2026 directly before quoting any figure from this entry. The outcome and the 260 to 98 division come from unofficial trackers only; no official source was retrievable in this run. Do not put the division numbers in a board paper or compliance document on this basis.

Build third-party assurance now against the Bill's direction of travel, not its final text. Every substantive version has pointed the same way: wider scope, managed service providers and designated critical suppliers in scope, supplier accountability, faster incident reporting. None of that requires the final wording to start on.

Use today's report as the evidence base for that board paper. Five of ten entries turn on third-party exposure: Gatwick through Times24 UK Limited, Next plc through an unnamed supplier, Juniper SD-WAN through managed service providers, N-able MailAssure through the MSP channel, and refrigeration controllers owned by facilities contractors. The argument for supply chain investment does not need the statute; it needs this week.

Read the 29 April 2027 carry-over extension as the absence of a forcing deadline, and plan accordingly. There is no near-term regulatory event that will compel action, while the underlying risk accumulates at the rate the rest of this report documents. Organisations waiting for the statutory duty will wait through at least one more winter of these incidents.

If you are a UK managed service provider or a supplier to designated operators, start the work now regardless of the Bill's progress. Your customers are already asking the questions this report recommends they ask - see ranks 3, 4, 7 and 9 - and being able to answer them is a commercial advantage well before it is a legal duty.

Track the Bill at bills.parliament.uk/bills/4035 rather than through press coverage. The ping-pong stage moves on parliamentary scheduling, not news cycles, and the next Lords consideration date is the thing to watch. Assign someone to own it.

Separate the two amendments when briefing: Amendment 107 (yearly NIS review) is an operational governance mechanism that affects how quickly the regime adapts; Amendment 108 (register of foreign powers) is a transparency and attribution question. Conflating them produces a muddled brief, and only one of them changes your compliance workload.

For UK CNI operators in the transport, health, energy, water and digital sectors: identify now which of your suppliers would be designated critical suppliers under any plausible version of this Bill, and begin assurance with those first. That list is also, independently, your highest-risk third-party population today.

Note the posture context when assessing nation-state risk in your own threat model. The UK publicly confirmed offensive cyber operations against Russia, China, Iran and North Korea in this same month, on 20 and around 23 November. That is relevant to UK organisations' exposure to retaliatory and opportunistic state-aligned activity, independently of the Bill.

Do not treat this entry as non-actionable because it has no CVE. The NCSC recorded 80 nationally significant incidents and stated on 3 November that UK cyber resilience is falling behind. The regime that is supposed to address that is still in ping-pong with a backstop five months away. That gap is a risk to record on the register, with a named owner.

kql.name: Build the designated-supplier inventory the Bill will require
kql.description: The Bill's direction of travel is managed service providers and designated critical suppliers in scope. This produces the observed third-party connectivity inventory that any version of that duty will need.
kql.query:
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where isnotempty(DestinationHostName)
| extend IsExternalDest = not(ipv4_is_private(DestinationIP))
| where IsExternalDest
| summarize Sessions = count(), BytesOut = sum(toint(coalesce(SentBytes, 0))), InternalSources = dcount(SourceIP), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by DestinationHostName
| where InternalSources > 2
| extend SustainedRelationship = LastSeen - FirstSeen > 30d

kql.description: The supplier accountability question in identity terms: which external organisations can currently authenticate into your environment, and with what reach.
kql.query:
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where UserType == "Guest" or UserPrincipalName has "#EXT#"
| extend HomeDomain = tostring(split(tostring(split(UserPrincipalName, "#EXT#")[0]), "_")[-1])
| summarize Signins = count(), Successes = countif(ResultType == 0), Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 25), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by HomeDomain
| order by Successes desc

kql.name: Privileged access granted to external and supplier principals
kql.description: What the regime will ask you to evidence: which third parties hold privileged roles, who granted them and when. Produce the record before anyone asks for it.
kql.query:
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(180d)
| where OperationName has_any ("Add member to role", "Add eligible member to role", "Add app role assignment", "Consent to application", "Add delegated permission grant")
| extend Target = tostring(TargetResources[0].userPrincipalName), TargetApp = tostring(TargetResources[0].displayName), Actor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName)
| where Target has "#EXT#" or isnotempty(TargetApp)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, Target, TargetApp, Actor, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

summary_statistics.third_party_compromise_pattern_this_mont: FIVE FOR FIVE. Every confirmed UK consumer-facing compromise disclosed in November 2026 originated at a third party, not at the named brand: Optimizely's signup flow serving malicious JavaScript from its own CDN to at least 178 organisations including the BBC, HSBC, TalkTalk, Zoom, IKEA, Salesforce and CNN (16 November); ASOS via third-party communications platforms; Next plc via an unnamed online supplier (23 November); TfL Oyster; and London Gatwick Airport via Times24 UK Limited, operator of its drop-off zones (24-25 November). Rank 8 extends the same failure mode one layer down the stack - 1Password's backend was reached through one hijacked employee GitHub account. Not one of these organisations was breached at its own perimeter, and not one could have prevented it by hardening its own estate. In at least two of the five the supplier was never named publicly, which is the difference between a scopable incident and an unscopable one.
summary_statistics.window_assessment: The most consequential item in this window is a CORRECTION TO YESTERDAY'S REPORT, not a new incident: Drupal SA-CORE-2026-019 / CVE-2026-136716, published 25 November, means the builds this feed told readers to deploy yesterday are insufficient, and Drupal's own warning that sites which kept the installer reachable after 18 November may already be compromised converts an eight-day window into an incident response trigger. The second feature of the window is volume and collision: ten new KEV entries on 25 November produced four new ranks in this report, and three separate KEV deadlines now fall inside 72 hours covering thirteen to fifteen exploited flaws across nine unrelated product families. Two deadlines expire TODAY. One deadline tomorrow cannot be met by patching at all, because Idunno.AntiCsrf has no patch and never will.
